generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, this means using the same habit on every assignment, whether it is a lab report, a coaching essay or a management piece. Whether you cite a study, a textbook or a governing body's guidance, you credit the idea, build the reference in your department's style, and check it is accurate. A physiology report and a coaching essay go through the same habit. Making this your normal way of working is what keeps your sport referencing trustworthy.
generatedProse.worked-example: Two sport students each use several sources in a report on a training programme. Tom pastes in ready-made references at the end and references only his direct quotations, leaving his paraphrased studies unmarked. Amara uses the whole habit: crediting each source as she uses it, building each reference from its parts in one style, and checking them for accuracy. Both knew the programme, but Amara's referencing is trustworthy, because she used every strand together.
generatedProse.summary: Referencing in the School of Sport is most useful when you treat it as one habit, not three separate ideas. On every assignment you run the same strands together: know why you credit a source, know its parts, and set it out accurately. Making this your normal way of working is what keeps your sport referencing trustworthy.

check.body: A student uses an author's idea in an essay. They put it in their own words, add an in-text reference, build it from its parts in their department's style, and check it is accurate. What does this show?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following programme improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first programme, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next programme.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using the feedback fed back into the next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following programme improved: that is the cycle working.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student changed before the next programme, not the old mark or the deadline.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Using the feedback fed back into the student's next round of learning and preparation, which is why the next programme improved. The old mark cannot change and the deadline is not part of the cycle; feedback is not the end, it feeds the next turn.

_items.text: That the student is using the whole referencing habit: knowing it is needed, building it from its parts, and setting it out accurately.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three strands are there, working together as one habit.

_items.text: That the student is doing more than referencing a source needs.
_items.feedback: No. Each part does a different job, and together they make the reference trustworthy.

_items.text: That only the in-text reference really matters.
_items.feedback: Not so. Crediting, the parts and accuracy all matter together.

_items.text: That paraphrasing does not need a reference.
_items.feedback: A paraphrase needs a reference just as a quotation does.
